content: 1. Ensure uninterrupted and free access to high-quality, quality-assured medicines for patients. 2. Guarantee appropriate access to healthcare services at the lowest possible direct and indirect costs. 3. Expand the supplier base for antileishmanial diagnostic tests and medicines to improve availability. 4. Strengthen the relevant health infrastructure and enhance the capacity of human resources to manage cases effectively. 5. Improve coordination among programs addressing HIV, visceral leishmaniasis (VL), and related conditions, such as pharmacovigilance, tuberculosis (TB), and vector control initiatives. 6. Routinely screen VL patients for HIV and ensure follow-up care, including screening for TB at the time of VL diagnosis. 7. Conduct long-term follow-up of treated patients to better understand the development of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), monitor HIV viral load, and assess nutritional status, including dietary modifications. 8. Address the importance of co-morbid conditions in VL-HIV patients, such as TB, and study their impact further. 9. Conduct basic research to understand the immunological interactions between VL and HIV infections and the immune-modulatory effects of drugs, which could improve co-infection management. 10. Develop and implement operational research to create effective screening strategies in areas with high HIV-VL prevalence and integrate relevant components of VL and HIV programs. 11. Develop improved tests for cure and relapse monitoring, including better antigen detection tests and biomarkers to link clinical outcomes, relapse, parasitological status, and parasite resistance to medicines. 12. Conduct further clinical trials to evaluate the safety and efficacy of combination therapies for VL-HIV co-infection, particularly in field conditions in East Africa and South-East Asia. 13. Address the toxicity of current antileishmanial medicines and prioritize research into safer treatment regimens, as traditional pharmacovigilance approaches provide limited safety data. 14. Investigate the safety of miltefosine therapy beyond 28 days, as extended or repeated treatment cycles may be required for patients with multiple relapses. 15. Ensure access to contraception and pregnancy testing for women of childbearing potential before administering miltefosine, as it is contraindicated during pregnancy. 16. Provide comprehensive clinical management for VL-HIV patients, including adequate HIV treatment and nutritional support. 17. When miltefosine is unavailable or contraindicated, consider monotherapy with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) at a total dose of up to 40 mg/kg, following the recommended regimen. 18. Promote the use of combination therapy with L-AmB and miltefosine for VL-HIV co-infected patients in South-East Asia, as per WHO recommendations, while acknowledging the very low certainty of evidence supporting this approach. 19. Encourage the development of more user-friendly and oral antileishmanial medicines to improve treatment adherence and outcomes. 20. Address equity issues by ensuring the availability of treatment facilities, free provision of combination therapy, and access to quality-assured medicines, particularly in resource-limited settings. 21. Consider cultural acceptability, such as pregnancy testing among single women, and address patient beliefs about treatment efficacy to improve adherence and outcomes. 22. Ensure the feasibility of implementing interventions by addressing infrastructure, human resource availability, and training needs, particularly in high-burden areas. 23. Monitor and evaluate treatment outcomes, including the proportion of VL cases screened for HIV, the proportion of HIV-positive VL cases treated, and relapse rates within 6, 12, or 24 months. 24. Assess clinical cure rates, survival rates, and case fatality rates to determine the effectiveness of interventions and improve patient outcomes. 25. Balance the desirable and undesirable effects of interventions, considering cost-effectiveness, resource requirements, and health equity impacts. 26. Strengthen donation programs to ensure the long-term availability of essential medicines like L-AmB and reduce the burden on healthcare systems. 27. Implement region-specific treatment recommendations based on local epidemiology, such as the use of L-AmB and miltefosine in South Asia, where VL is caused by Leishmania donovani. 28. Encourage the use of combination therapy to reduce hospitalization duration and improve patient acceptability, while addressing potential disadvantages for women of childbearing potential. 29. Promote research to better understand the epidemiology and progression of VL in HIV patients, using improved biomarkers for earlier detection and better outcomes. 30. Advocate for well-designed studies to strengthen evidence for combination therapy and improve outcomes in field conditions in endemic regions.
